title: Year three close
hookLine: the long story is told; next year, the ways of the Guru: ragas, teachings, and the living panth

lines: A STORYTELLER, A WEAVER, A SERVANT.
cards: A storyteller's Nanak. A weaver's songs in the Guru's book. A servant sent north.
Families shielded in a moving ring. A gold roof, a boy far from home, protesters who didn't strike back, a kitchen that feeds whoever comes.
That's this year in one breath, from day six hundred ninety-seven, when Bhai Gurdas opened it, to this one. Each picture is a name that became a story.

teach.h: THREE YEARS: WORDS, A DAY, A MEMORY.
teach.b: Look at the shape of it. Year one gave you the path's words, stories, practices and the Japji. Year two gave you the daily banis, a day lived in the Guru's words.
Year three gave you a people's memory. It began with the tellers: Bhai Gurdas, Bhai Nand Lal, the janamsakhis, and the Bhagats. Then the people around the Gurus.
Then the hard century, the misls, the kingdom and its loss. Then reform, the twentieth century, and the calendar of days on which Sikhs remember. Why a whole year on history?
Listen to the Ardas. Before it asks for anything, it remembers: the Gurus by name, the four Sahibzade, the five beloved ones, the forty liberated ones, and the martyrs who kept their faith.

teach.h: THE ARDAS TELLS THE STORY AGAIN.
teach.b: Every time a Sikh stands for the Ardas, the long story is told again in a few minutes. So the history isn't a school subject sitting beside the faith.
It's inside the prayer. Whoever stands for the Ardas stands among everyone it names: the story holds us. Now turn and face the other way.

teach.h: YEAR FOUR: THE WAYS OF THE GURU.
teach.b: Year four is the ways of the Guru: the ragas the Granth is set in, the teachings opened slowly, and the living panth, the community as it lives now.
Tomorrow begins with a question about sound, and why the Gurus' words were meant to be sung. This year's faces won't vanish. Bhai Gurdas's vars, for one, are sung in kirtan beside the Guru's words.

how: In the Ardas, said standing at the end of Sikh prayers and gatherings, Sikhs remember the Gurus, the Sahibzade, the Panj Pyare, the forty liberated ones and the martyrs before making their requests, so the community's history is recalled every time it is said.

o: regret for the hard things that happened this year
a way to leave the old stories behind for good
seeing a whole year of a people's memory at once

practice: Lean back, let the shoulders drop, and for a while do nothing at all while the year settles: the tellers, the martyrs, the kings, the exiles, the kitchens.

Toward the end, look forward to a sound: a harmonium, a voice, a line of the Guru's words set to music. If you pray, say Waheguru once, as thanks for the year; if you don't, simply let tomorrow have some room in it.

wordCard.voice: Ardas. The standing prayer that remembers the long story, the tellers, the saints, the hard century, the kingdom and its loss, renewal and today, before it asks for anything. Today's word.
